title: Implicit and explicit values

draft.title: Implicit and explicit values
card: Values are beliefs about what matters or what is right. Attitudes are the feelings a writer or speaker shows towards a topic or person.
stated outright. For example, 'Public libraries are essential to every town.'
hidden in word choice, examples and assumptions. Calling a plan 'reckless' or only describing the benefits of an idea suggests an attitude without stating it.
To spot a value, ask what the text treats as good, bad or normal, and which words or examples show this.
draft.remember: Values can be stated outright or hinted at through the words, examples and assumptions a text uses.

a.q: Which sentence shows an implicit value about city living?
opts: Escaping the noisy, crowded city at last, Tom breathed again
I believe city life is worse than country life
City life is worse than country life, and everyone knows it
Tom decided that he preferred country life to city life
a.why: The words 'noisy', 'crowded' and 'breathed again' suggest the city is unpleasant without saying so directly. The other options state a preference outright, so those values are explicit.
a.clue: Which one hints at an opinion without stating it?

b.q: An article about a new skate park describes teenagers as 'loitering' and the council as 'responsibly' spending money. What is the implicit attitude?
opts: Teenagers are a problem and the council is trustworthy
Skate parks are a waste of public money
Teenagers and the council are equally to blame
The writer has no attitude and reports only facts
b.why: 'Loitering' casts teenagers negatively and 'responsibly' praises the council, so the word choice shows the attitude. The text never says skate parks are a waste, so that is not supported. Neutral-sounding reporting can still carry an attitude.
b.clue: Look at the one word used for each group.

a.best: Escaping the noisy, crowded city at last, Tom breathed again

b.best: Teenagers are a problem and the council is trustworthy
